chapters.title: From traders to rulers (1757–1805)
chapters.intro:
In 1756 the English East India Company was a trading company with a few forts on the coast. By 1805 it ruled Bengal, Bihar, Orissa, coastal Andhra and Rayalaseema, controlled Awadh and Hyderabad, had destroyed Tipu Sultan, and held Delhi.

Read this chapter year by year. Watch three threads: **Bengal** (Plassey, Buxar, the Diwani), **the south** (the four Mysore wars), and **the Marathas** (Salbai to Bassein). Notice how each victory brought money, and how the money paid for the next war.
takeaways: Plassey (1757) gave political power; Buxar (1764) and the Diwani (1765) made it legal and paid for it.
Mysore fought four wars (1767–69, 1780–84, 1790–92, 1799); Tipu died in 1799.
The First Anglo-Maratha War ended at Salbai (1782) with no clear winner; Bassein (1802) led to the second war.
The Subsidiary Alliance (1798) brought states under control without war; the Nizam was first.
Andhra came to the Company in two pieces: the Northern Circars (1766) and the Ceded Districts (1800).
chapters.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2–3; NCERT Class 12 Themes III, Ch. 9

fragments.title: Bengal passes to the Company
fragments.intro: A new nawab picks a fight with the Company. Ten years later the Company collects Bengal's revenue. Meanwhile, in the north, an Afghan king smashes the Marathas.

fragments.title: Hastings, Haidar and the Marathas
fragments.intro: The Company takes coastal Andhra, Parliament starts to control it, and it fights Mysore and the Marathas at the same time.

fragments.title: Cornwallis to Wellesley
fragments.intro: Cornwallis fixes Bengal's land revenue for ever. Wellesley's Subsidiary Alliance and two wars finish Tipu and humble the Marathas.

chapters.title: The Company becomes paramount (1806–1857)
chapters.intro:
By 1805 the Company was the strongest power in India. In the next fifty years it finished off the Marathas, made itself 'paramount' over every Indian state, conquered Sindh and the Punjab, and annexed state after state under Dalhousie.

At the same time it changed how India was governed — land revenue, laws, English education, social reforms — and resistance kept breaking out: Vellore, Khurda, Kittur, the Kols, the Santhals. In 1857 it all came together in a great revolt.

fragments.title: Vellore to the fall of the Peshwa
fragments.intro: Sepoys rise at Vellore, the Sutlej becomes a border, Nepal is beaten, the Paiks of Khurda revolt, and the last Peshwa loses his throne.

fragments.title: Reform and resistance
fragments.intro: New land revenue systems, the first Burmese war, Rani Channamma of Kittur, the abolition of sati, and English education.

fragments.title: Afghanistan, Sindh and the Sikhs
fragments.intro: Fear of Russia drives the British into Afghanistan; then they take Sindh and, after Ranjit Singh dies, the Punjab.

fragments.title: Dalhousie and the road to 1857
fragments.intro: Railways, telegraph and the Doctrine of Lapse; the Santhals rise; Awadh is annexed; and in 1857 the sepoys revolt.

takeaways: Paramountcy (Lord Hastings, 1813–23): the Company claimed supreme authority over all Indian states (NCERT).
The Peshwa was removed in 1818 after the Third Anglo-Maratha War (1817–19) (NCERT).
Afghan war 1838–42, Sindh 1843, Punjab 1849 (NCERT).
Doctrine of Lapse: Satara 1848, Sambalpur 1850, Udaipur 1852, Nagpur 1853, Jhansi 1854; Awadh taken in 1856 (NCERT).
Resistance before 1857: Vellore 1806, Khurda 1817, Kittur 1824, Kols 1831–32, Santhals 1855 (NCERT).
chapters.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 2–7; NCERT Class 12 Themes III, Ch. 10–11

chapters.title: The Crown, reform and the birth of nationalism (1858–1905)
chapters.intro:
After 1857 the British Crown took over India from the Company. Viceroys now ruled for the Queen, and the British promised not to annex more states. But land revenue, famines and racial arrogance went on.

In these fifty years Indians organised in new ways: reform societies (Arya Samaj, Satyashodhak Samaj, Aligarh), peasant and tribal revolts (indigo, Deccan, Birsa Munda), and political associations that led to the Indian National Congress (1885). Curzon's partition of Bengal (1905) ends the chapter and starts a new kind of struggle.

fragments.title: The Crown takes over
fragments.intro: The Queen's Proclamation, new councils and laws, the indigo revolt, and the first reform societies of the new age.

fragments.title: Lytton, Ripon and the first associations
fragments.intro: A famine and a grand Durbar, the "gagging" press act, then a liberal Viceroy — and the Ilbert Bill storm.

fragments.title: The Congress is born
fragments.intro: The Indian National Congress meets in Bombay; reformers, writers and a monk at Chicago change how Indians see themselves.

fragments.title: Birsa Munda and Curzon's India
fragments.intro: Birsa leads the Mundas; Curzon reorganises everything — and partitions Bengal.

takeaways: Government of India Act 1858: power passed from the Company to the Crown (NCERT).
Indigo revolt 1859–60; Deccan riots 1875; Birsa Munda 1895–1900 (NCERT).
Arms Act and Vernacular Press Act 1878; Ilbert Bill controversy 1883 (NCERT).
INC founded by 72 delegates at Bombay in December 1885 (NCERT).
Curzon partitioned Bengal in 1905 (NCERT).
chapters.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 3–8; NCERT Class 12 Themes III, Ch. 10

chapters.title: The freedom struggle (1906–1947)
chapters.intro:
From the Swadeshi movement to 15 August 1947. After 1919 the struggle became a mass movement of peasants, tribals, students, women and workers (NCERT), led above all by Mahatma Gandhi.

Follow four threads year by year: the Congress and its movements (Non-Cooperation, Civil Disobedience, Quit India); the revolutionaries (Ghadar, HSRA, INA); British reforms (1909, 1919, 1935) and their failures; and the growing Hindu–Muslim divide that ended in Partition. Andhra's own story — Vandemataram, the Andhra Mahasabha, Alluri, Chirala-Perala and Pedanandipadu — runs alongside.

fragments.title: Swadeshi to the Great War
fragments.intro: Swadeshi spreads, the Congress splits, the League is born, Bengal is reunited, Ghadar rises abroad, and Gandhi comes home.

fragments.title: Gandhi's first mass movements
fragments.intro: Rowlatt and Jallianwala, Khilafat and Non-Cooperation, Alluri in the Rampa hills, the Simon boycott and the call for Purna Swaraj.

fragments.title: Civil Disobedience and provincial rule
fragments.intro: The Salt March, the Round Table Conferences, the Poona Pact, the 1935 Act and Congress ministries.

fragments.title: Quit India to independence
fragments.intro: War, the Pakistan resolution, Cripps, Quit India, the INA, the Cabinet Mission — and freedom with Partition.

takeaways: Muslim League 1906; Congress split 1907; separate electorates 1909; Lucknow Pact 1916 (NCERT).
Gandhi returned in 1915; Champaran, Kheda and Ahmedabad came first (NCERT).
Rowlatt satyagraha and Jallianwala Bagh 1919; Non-Cooperation 1920–22, ended after Chauri Chaura (NCERT).
Purna Swaraj 1929; Dandi March 1930; 1935 Act; Congress ministries 1937 in 7 of 11 provinces (NCERT).
Quit India 1942; INA 1944; Cabinet Mission 1946; Direct Action Day 16 August 1946; independence 1947 (NCERT).
chapters.source: NCERT Class 8 Our Pasts III, Ch. 8 "The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947"; NCERT Class 12 Themes III, Ch. 13–14

chapters.title: Independent India and Andhra Pradesh (1948–2014)
chapters.intro:
From Gandhi's assassination to the birth of Telangana. Independent India faced three challenges — unity, democracy and development (NCERT) — and then wars, the Emergency, coalitions and reforms.

Follow four threads year by year: nation-building (princely states, linguistic states, the North-East); democracy (elections, the Congress system, the Emergency, coalitions); development (Plans, the Green Revolution, 1991 reforms); and Andhra Pradesh — Potti Sriramulu, Andhra State, the Gentlemen's Agreement, 1969 and 1972, NTR, and the 2014 bifurcation. Major court cases and amendments are placed in the year they happened.

fragments.title: Building the nation
fragments.intro: Gandhi is killed, Hyderabad and Manipur join, the Constitution comes into force, India votes for the first time, Potti Sriramulu dies for Andhra, and states are redrawn by language.

fragments.title: Nehru's later years to Shastri
fragments.intro: Kerala's Communist government, Panchayati Raj, the Indus treaty, Goa, the China war, Nehru's death, the 1965 war, Tashkent and the Green Revolution.

fragments.title: Indira, war and the Emergency
fragments.intro: The 1967 shock, Telangana 1969, the Congress split, bank nationalisation, Bangladesh, Simla, Jai Andhra and the Six-Point Formula, Kesavananda, the Emergency and the Janata interlude.

fragments.title: Indira's return to the 1991 reforms
fragments.intro: NTR's Telugu Desam, Blue Star and Indira Gandhi's assassination, Bhopal, the accords of Rajiv Gandhi, the 1989 coalition, Mandal, Rajiv Gandhi's assassination and the 1991 reforms.

fragments.title: Coalitions and a new Andhra
fragments.intro: Panchayati Raj in the Constitution, Ayodhya, coalitions, Pokhran-II and Kargil, three new states, the TRS, the UPA years, the Telangana movement and the bifurcation of Andhra Pradesh.

takeaways: Gandhi assassinated 30 January 1948; Operation Polo September 1948; Constitution adopted 26 November 1949, in force 26 January 1950 (NCERT).
Potti Sriramulu died 15 December 1952 after 56 days; Andhra State 1 October 1953 (Kurnool); SRC 1953; Gentlemen's Agreement 20 February 1956; Andhra Pradesh 1 November 1956.
Panchsheel 1954; NAM Belgrade 1961; wars 1962, 1965, 1971; Tashkent 1966; Simla 1972 (NCERT).
1967 earthquake; Congress split 1969; Emergency 25 June 1975 – March 1977; Janata 1977 (NCERT).
Telangana agitation 1969; Jai Andhra 1972; Six-Point Formula 1973 and Article 371-D.
TDP 1982 and NTR CM 1983; 1989 end of the Congress system; Mandal 1990; reforms 1991 (NCERT).
73rd/74th Amendments 1992; Kargil 1999; three new states 2000; TRS 2001; AP Reorganisation Act 2014 and Telangana on 2 June 2014.
chapters.source: NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 1 "Challenges of Nation Building"; NCERT Class 12 Politics in India since Independence, Ch. 2–8; AP SCERT / Telugu Akademi
